[MUQATIL:28:8-11/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Pharaoh’s household found Moses in his chest among water and trees; Muqatil derives his name from Coptic mo (water) and si (tree).
[MUQATIL:28:8-11/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Moses would be their enemy through their destruction and a source of grief and anger over the killing of their firstborn; linked to 26:55. | mentions 26:55
[MUQATIL:28:8-11/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Muqatil repeats the verse’s judgment that Pharaoh, Haman, and their troops were wrongdoers.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p578#2/r10] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda explains that Moses opposed them in religion and brought them grief.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p578#2/r11] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | Pharaoh, Hāmān, and their troops were polytheists.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p578#2/r9] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · يحيى | reports | Yaḥyā says the only report he heard was that washerwomen on the Nile picked Moses up.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p328#5/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | The family did not adopt Moses at that moment in order to make him an enemy; they took him as a son, and the concise wording says he later became their enemy and grief.
[TUSTARI:28:8/r1] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Pharaoh's household took Moses in expecting joy and delight, unaware that divine power had destined him to become their enemy and grief.
[TAB-FULL:v18p159/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī explains iltiqāṭ as an unexpected meeting or finding, without seeking the thing beforehand.
[TAB-FULL:v18p159/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الراجز | reports | An anonymous rajaz verse uses iltiqāṭ to describe unexpectedly reaching a watering place, witnessing the sense of sudden encounter.
[TAB-FULL:v18p159/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī says Asiya's maidservants found the chest among trees near Pharaoh's house, brought it to her thinking it held treasure, and she loved the baby and persuaded Pharaoh not to kill him despite his fear that Moses was an Israelite child who would destroy them.
[TAB-FULL:v18p159/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · محمد بن قيس | reports | Muḥammad ibn Qays says Pharaoh's daughter, who was afflicted with leprosy, found the chest; looking at Moses cured her, and she declared him blessed and pleaded for his life. | mentions 28:9
[TAB-FULL:v18p159/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Isḥāq says Pharaoh's agents retrieved the chest after Asiya spotted it in the Nile; when they found the baby, God's love for him entered Pharaoh's heart and Asiya asked that they not kill him. | mentions 28:9
[TAB-FULL:v18p159/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī does not prefer one reported identification of Pharaoh's household over another; he retains the verse's general wording and refers back to his earlier explanation of āl. | mentions 2:49
[TAB-FULL:v18p162#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatādah glosses Moses as their enemy in religion and grief over what would befall them through him.
[TAB-FULL:v18p162#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قراء الكوفة | reports | Most Kufan readers read ḥuznan with ḍamma on ḥāʾ and sukūn on zāy.
[TAB-FULL:v18p162#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | With fatḥa, ḥazanan is the verbal noun of ḥazintu; with ḍamma and sukūn, ḥuzn is a noun, like the two forms al-ʿadam and al-ʿudm.
[TAB-FULL:v18p162#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī regards the two readings as close in meaning and both correct, like the variants al-ʿadam and al-ʿudm.
[TAB-FULL:v18p162/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The lām describes the eventual outcome, not the purpose for which Pharaoh's people took Moses: they thought he would benefit them, but his eventual role brought their destruction, as God had willed.
[TAB-FULL:v18p162/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Isḥāq explains that Moses became their enemy and grief in the final outcome of his affair, by God's will, although that was not why they took him.
[TAB-FULL:v18p162/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | He compares the wording to rebuking someone whose apparently beneficial act ultimately harms him: they took Moses expecting comfort, but the outcome was their ruin at his hands.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p132/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | The phrase is also read with the alternative vocalization حَزَنًا alongside حُزْنًا.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p132/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The clause describes an outcome, not their intention; it is like acquiring wealth that leads to one's death.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p492/r2] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Hamza and al-Kisāʾī use ḍamma on ḥāʾ and sukūn on zāy in حزن; the others use fatḥa on both.
[IBNABIHATIM:v9p2943/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أبو عبد الرحمن الحبلي | reports | Al-Hubuli reports that Pharaoh’s wife and her leprous daughter found the ark at sea; the daughter opened it, took Moses, and was cured.
[IBNABIHATIM:v9p2943/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عمر بن عبد العزيز | reports | In a letter defending God’s prior decree, ʿUmar argues Moses was destined to become Pharaoh’s enemy and sorrow; this rebuts the claim that Pharaoh could have been his supporter. He cites God’s instruction to Moses and Aaron. | mentions 20:43
[IBNABIHATIM:v9p2943/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · محمد بن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Isḥāq says Moses became Pharaoh’s enemy in the eventual outcome, as God willed; that outcome was not why Pharaoh’s household adopted him.
[IBNABIHATIM:v9p2943/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Isḥāq describes Pharaoh as exceptionally rebellious, outspoken, and long-reigning among his people, and reports his name as al-Walīd ibn Muṣʿab.
[IBNABIHATIM:v9p2943/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says Pharaoh was a non-Arab from Hamadhān.
[IBNABIHATIM:v9p2943/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī says Hāmān led Pharaoh’s vanguard with 1,700,000 horses.
[NAHHAS:v3p227/r11] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | ليكون is accusative under the purpose lām; the construction is ordinary Arabic, even if weak grammarians object to it.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p412/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Hamza and al-Kisai read حُزنا with ḍamma on ح; the remaining readers use fatḥa on both ح and ز.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p412/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | حُزن and حَزَن are two regular dialect forms with the same meaning, like العجم/العجم and العرب/العرب.
[BAQILLANI:v1p102/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Bāqillānī defines tadhyīl as emphatic reinforcement, opposite to allusion, and gives the Pharaoh narrative through the Israelites' inheritance as a Quranic example.
[SULAMI:v2p100#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · سهل | reports | Sahl says Pharaoh’s household picked Moses up expecting joy, unaware that divine decree had hidden his becoming their enemy and grief.
[THALABI:v7p235/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Pharaoh's only, beloved daughter had severe leprosy; doctors and magicians said a child found from the sea would heal her if his saliva were applied at a specified sunrise.
[THALABI:v7p235/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | On the appointed Monday, Pharaoh and Asiya sat by the Nile as the princess played at its bank; servants retrieved the chest, but could neither open nor break it.
[THALABI:v7p235/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Asiya alone saw a light inside the chest and opened it; Moses lay in a cradle with light between his eyes, and God provided milk through his thumb.
[THALABI:v7p235/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | God placed love for Moses in Asiya's heart; Pharaoh also loved him, and the princess's application of his saliva cured her leprosy, so she embraced him.
[THALABI:v7p235/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Pharaoh's advisers suspected Moses was the Israelite child feared by the regime and had been cast into the river to escape him; Pharaoh moved to kill the baby.
[THALABI:v7p235/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Asiya pleaded that Moses might benefit them or be adopted as a son; she was childless and asked Pharaoh for him, so Pharaoh gave him to her while saying he himself had no need of the child.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p236/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas says the Pharaoh's wife's attendants found the infant's chest when they went out to draw water and carried it to her.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p236/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · عبد الرحمن بن زيد | reports | ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd says Pharaoh's wife, who had leprosy, found the chest at the sea, took the infant, and was cured; she called him blessed.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p236/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The verse names the eventual outcome as if it were already present: Moses was not then an enemy or grief, since Pharaoh's wife rejoiced in and deeply loved him.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p236/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الشاعر | reports | The cited anonymous poetic line about death nurturing every nursing mother illustrates naming a present state by its eventual outcome.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p336/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Pharaoh’s household found Moses in the sea; the verb means coming upon an object without having sought it.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p336/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المفسرون | reports | The people of Pharaoh here are his wife’s maidservants, who took Moses’ chest from the sea.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p336/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The two readings huznan and huzunan are dialectal variants, like the paired forms saqam and Arab.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p336/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abu Ishaq says the phrase describes the eventual outcome, not the family’s purpose in taking Moses; the cited verse likewise does not mean mothers give birth intending death.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p336/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil glosses the outcome as Moses becoming their enemy in their destruction and a source of grief in their hearts.

[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:28:7-10/r3] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Pharaoh’s household took Moses from the water; the outcome was that he became their enemy and grief.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:28:7-10/r4] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Pharaoh, Haman, and their troops were disobedient and sinful.
[DAMGHANI:v1p157/r8] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Khāṭiʾūn can mean sinners guilty of shirk; the same applies to the people who do not eat from the tree in Hell. | mentions 69:37
[JISHUMI:v3p2244#2/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The Pharaoh-family phrase فالتقطه آل فرعون ليكون لهم عدوا وحزنا is cited as another example of a consequential lām. | mentions 28:8
[JISHUMI:v8p5470#2/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ḥuznan with ḍamma on ḥāʾ and still zāy; others use fatḥa on both. Both are lexical variants.
[JISHUMI:v8p5470#2/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Iltiqāṭ is finding something without having sought it, as with a lost object.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p193/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · آسية | reports | The account says Āsiya named the child Mūsā because they found him among water and trees, glossing the name’s parts as water and tree.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p398/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The لام in ليكون is the purposive لام كي, expressing cause.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p398/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The causality is metaphorical: Pharaoh's family picked Moses up from affection and adoption, but the result is presented as though it motivated the act.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p398/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The metaphor is like presenting an outcome as a cause, as in coming “to honor me” or striking someone “so he may be disciplined.”
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p398/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | حزنا and حُزنا are two language forms, like العدم and العدم.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p398/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | خاطئين may mean Pharaoh's people were wrong in everything, so raising their enemy was typical of them.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p398/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Alternatively, they were criminals whom God punished by making them raise their own enemy and destroyer.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p398/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | A reading has خاطين, either a shortened form of خاطئين or meaning those who strayed from right into error.
[TABRISI:28:8/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās recounts that the midwife loved and warned Moses’ mother; his sister hid him in a lit furnace God cooled; later a carpenter’s failed attempts to expose the mother signaled divine intervention.
[TABRISI:28:8/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Al-taqāṭ means Pharaoh’s household found and took Moses without seeking him.
[TABRISI:28:8/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The phrase describes the eventual outcome, not their purpose in taking Moses: a person may earn wealth that brings ruin without intending it.
[TABRISI:28:8/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Pharaoh, Hāmān, and their troops disobeyed God in their actions.
[TABRISI:28:8/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The Nile carried the chest to Pharaoh and his wife; Āsiya opened it and loved Moses. She was an Israelite of prophetic descent, compassionate and charitable to believers.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p233/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | جنود is the plural of جند and denotes a large gathered number.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p233/r5] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | A fourth sense is assembled multitudes, including Pharaoh, Haman and their troops.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p271/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | reports | Khaṭaʾ can mean associating partners with God. | mentions 69:37
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p198#3/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الحسن وعطاء وعكرمة | reports | Hasan, Ata, and Ikrima hold that all of al-Qasas is Meccan.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p203/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Picking up means finding or taking something without having sought it.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p203/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says Pharaoh's female attendants took the ark from the water.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p203/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · محمد بن قيس | reports | Muhammad ibn Qays says Pharaoh's daughter took the ark.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p203/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن إسحاق | reports | Ibn Ishaq says Pharaoh's agents took the ark.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p203/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | This is the lām of consequence: the outcome was that Moses became their enemy, not why they took him; the explanation was given in Yunus.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p203/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · المفسرون | reports | One view makes Moses an enemy to their religion and a grief because of what he did to them.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p203/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · المفسرون | reports | Another view makes him an enemy to their men and grief for their women: men were drowned and women enslaved.
[RAZI-FULL:v24p195/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Iltiqāṭ means finding or picking something up without having sought it; the family of Pharaoh here means his female servants.
[RAZI-FULL:v24p195/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The commonly held view takes the lām as one of consequence; a purpose reading would conflict with Pharaoh’s wife calling Moses a comfort and God’s saying He cast love on him, as in 7:179. | mentions 28:9, 20:39, 7:179
[RAZI-FULL:v24p195/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · صاحب الكشاف | prefers | Rāzī prefers al-Zamakhsharī’s account: this is figurative purpose, since an object’s eventual outcome is treated as its aim, like calling a brave person a lion.
[RAZI-FULL:v24p195/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The poem “They bear children for death and build for ruin” illustrates a purpose construction whose result is the opposite of the apparent intent.
[RAZI-FULL:v24p195/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read ḥuznan with ḍamma on ḥāʾ and sukūn on zāy; the others read ḥazanan with fatḥa on both, two dialect forms like saqm and saqam.
[RAZI-FULL:v24p195/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says khāṭiʾīn here does not mean sinning: they did not realize this child would take their kingdom.
[RAZI-FULL:v24p195/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · جمهور المفسرين | reports | Most exegetes understand that Pharaoh’s people were wrong in disbelief and oppression, so God made them raise their enemy, the cause of their destruction, themselves.
[RAZI-FULL:v24p195/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A shortened reading, khāṭīn, lightens khāṭiʾīn and means those who miss the right and go toward error.
[QURTUBI-FULL:28:7-8/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | التقاط is finding something without seeking or intending it; Arabic also uses the verb for an accidental encounter, and the legal discussion of found property was treated in Surat Yusuf.
[QURTUBI-FULL:28:7-8/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The lām marks consequence, not the family's intention: they took Moses hoping for joy, but the outcome was that he became their enemy and grief.
[QURTUBI-FULL:28:7-8/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · شاعر | reports | An unnamed poet illustrates the consequence construction by saying that every nursing mother nurtures someone destined for death and every home is built for ruin.
[QURTUBI-FULL:28:7-8/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · شاعر | reports | A second unnamed poet likewise says mothers raise children for death and houses are built for destruction, demonstrating outcome rather than intent.
[QURTUBI-FULL:28:8-9/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The poetic phrase منهلا وردته التقاطا illustrates an accidental finding; the word is also the source of luqata, lost property, whose rules were discussed in Surat Yusuf.
[QURTUBI-FULL:28:8-9/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الأعمش ويحيى والمفضل وحمزة والكسائي وخلف | reports | These readers pronounce حزنًا with ḍamma on ḥāʾ and sukūn on zāy; the remaining readers use fatḥa on both, which Abu ʿUbayd selects, and Abu Hatim favors emphatic pronunciation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:28:8-9/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The two pronunciations are dialectal forms, like the variant pairs for want, sickness, and right guidance.
[QURTUBI-FULL:28:8-9/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Haman was Pharaoh's minister and was a Copt.
[QURTUBI-FULL:28:8-9/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The verse calls Pharaoh, Haman, and their troops disobedient, polytheistic sinners.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:28:7-8/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The clause about his becoming their enemy and grief explains the outcome of their taking him, presented as though it were their motive.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:28:7-8/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Hamza and al-Kisāʾī read حزنًا.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:28:7-8/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | They were wrong in everything: after killing thousands to find Moses, they raised him to maturity so he could do what they feared; the sentence emphasizes their error or explains their affliction.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:28:7-8/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, they were sinners, and God punished them by having them raise their enemy themselves.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:28:7-8/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | A reading خاطين lightens خطئين; another has خاطين, those who make error in place of correctness.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p227#3/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Al-taqaṭahu means that Pharaoh's people took the child.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p227#3/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says Pharaoh was Persian, from Istakhr.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p227#3/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj takes the outcome as the sense: they did not take Moses in order to make him their enemy; events came to that end, as in the saying about a child being born for death.

10 · المفسرون | reports | The commentators call the lām the lām of consequence or eventual outcome.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p227#3/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | The author of al-Kashshāf calls it a purpose lām, but says its causal sense is figurative because the outcome of their taking him resembles a motive for it.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p227#3/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · حمزة | reports | Hamza reads the alternate form ḥuzn; both forms are Arabic variants, like the two forms of ʿadam.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p227#3/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abu Jaʿfar lightens the hamza in the reading of khāṭiʾīn.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p227#3/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | They were sinners, and God punished them by raising their enemy and eventual destroyer in their own household; their wrongdoing in everything made this outcome typical of them.
[QASHANI:28:7-8/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Pharaoh's family represents the dominant psychic faculties; discernment and protection require the aid of imagination, estimation, and the outer and inner senses.
[QASHANI:28:7-8/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Ultimately a person learns that his fiercest enemy is the self between his sides, then subdues its helpers by discipline and annihilates it through restraint, breaking, and mortification.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p286#2/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | An omitted sequence says she nursed Moses and cast him into the river; li-yakuna describes the eventual consequence of Pharaoh's family taking him, although they intended adoption and affection.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p286#2/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Most read huznan with both vowels open, a Quraysh dialect; several named readers use a damma on ha and sukun on za.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p286#2/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A khatiʾ commits error deliberately, unlike a mukhtiʾ; the likely omitted sense is that Moses became their enemy and grief because they persisted in crimes and unbelief.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p287/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المبرد | reports | Al-Mubarrad says Pharaoh's family wronged themselves by taking Moses; other explanations blame killing Israelite children or raising their enemy.
